answer: Glaucoma is a group of diseases that can damage the eye's optic nerve and result in vision loss and blindness.
It is often caused by a buildup of fluid that increases pressure in the eye, damaging the nerve fibers.
The most common type, open-angle glaucoma, initially has no symptoms and causes no pain; vision seems normal.
While it cannot be cured, it can be controlled with eye drops, laser surgery, or conventional surgery.
African-Americans over age 40 and everyone over age 60 are at a higher risk for developing the condition.
There is no known way to prevent glaucoma, but early detection through dilated eye exams can save vision.
Doctors diagnose glaucoma by performing a comprehensive dilated eye exam to look at the optic nerve.
The National Eye Institute is researching gene therapy and new medications to better protect the optic nerve.
Open-angle glaucoma is the most common form where fluid leaves the eye too slowly, causing pressure build-up.
The optic nerve is a bundle of more than 1 million nerve fibers connecting the retina to the brain.
Without treatment, people with glaucoma will slowly lose their peripheral vision, resulting in tunnel vision.
Immediate treatment for early-stage glaucoma can delay progression and prevent further damage.
Nearly 2.7 million people in the U.S. have glaucoma, making it a leading cause of blindness.
Family history plays a significant role; those with a parent or sibling with glaucoma are at higher risk.
High-risk individuals should have a comprehensive dilated eye exam at least once every two years.
Damage to the optic nerve fibers stops the transmission of visual information from the retina to the brain.
Angle-closure glaucoma is a less common form that can cause a sudden, painful rise in eye pressure.
Laser trabeculoplasty helps fluid drain out of the eye to lower intraocular pressure.
Tonometry is a standard test used during an eye exam to measure the internal pressure of the eye.
It refers to a group of eye conditions that lead to irreversible damage to the optic nerve.
High blood pressure is a condition where blood flows through arteries at higher than normal pressures.
It is often called the "silent killer" because it typically has no obvious symptoms for years.
Nearly 1 in 3 American adults have high blood pressure, and risk increases significantly with age.
Steps to prevent it include reducing salt intake, maintaining a healthy weight, and staying active.
Normal pressure is below 120/80 mmHg; higher readings indicate hypertension or prehypertension.
Treatment involves a combination of DASH diet, regular exercise, and blood pressure medications.
Changes in kidney function or blood vessel stiffness can cause pressure to rise over time.
Systolic (top number) is pressure during heartbeats; Diastolic (bottom) is pressure between beats.
For most adults, the goal of treatment is to keep blood pressure consistently below 140/90 mmHg.
Older adults should limit sodium to 1,500 mg per day, roughly 2/3 of a teaspoon of salt.
Blood pressure rises with weight; losing even 10 pounds can significantly lower pressure levels.
The DASH diet emphasizes fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy to help stop hypertension.
African Americans tend to develop high blood pressure earlier in life and have more severe cases.
Left untreated, it can lead to damaged arteries, stroke, heart failure, and kidney disease.
A blood pressure cuff, or sphygmomanometer, is the primary tool used for diagnosis.
A family history of hypertension increases the likelihood that an individual will develop the disease.
Diuretics, or water pills, are a common medicine that helps the kidneys remove salt and water.
Beta blockers help the heart beat slower and with less force, lowering overall blood pressure.
Limiting alcohol consumption is a key lifestyle change to prevent and manage hypertension.
Many doctors recommend home monitoring to track pressure changes throughout the day.
Diabetes means your blood glucose (blood sugar) is too high because the body cannot process it properly.
Type 1 is an autoimmune disease where the body attacks cells that make insulin, requiring daily shots.
Type 2 occurs when the body doesn't make or use insulin well; it is the most common form.
Symptoms include extreme thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, and blurry vision.
It cannot be cured but is managed through blood sugar monitoring, diet, and medication.
Risk factors for Type 2 include being over 45, being overweight, and lack of physical activity.
Long-term high blood sugar can damage nerves (neuropathy) and blood vessels throughout the body.
People with prediabetes can prevent Type 2 by losing weight and increasing physical activity.
It is often silent; serious complications can occur before a person even knows they have it.
People with Type 1 must use insulin shots or an insulin pump to stay alive and healthy.
The A1C test measures your average blood sugar levels over the past three months.
Aerobic activities like walking help the body use insulin better and lower blood glucose.
Managing the amount of carbohydrates eaten is essential for keeping blood sugar in range.
Heart disease and stroke are the leading causes of death for people living with diabetes.
Having a parent or sibling with diabetes increases your risk of developing the disease.
People with diabetes must check their feet daily for sores to prevent serious infections.
Regular finger-prick tests or continuous glucose monitors help track daily sugar fluctuations.
Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar that develops during pregnancy and usually goes away after.
Many with Type 2 take pills like metformin to help their bodies use insulin more effectively.
Diabetes is a leading cause of kidney disease, which can lead to the need for dialysis.
Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis, resulting from the wear and tear of joint cartilage.
It is caused by years of mechanical stress on joints, most often affecting hands, knees, and hips.
Warning signs include joint pain, tenderness, and stiffness after periods of inactivity.
Treatment goals are to manage pain and improve function through exercise and heat therapy.
It is estimated that over 33% of people over age 65 are affected by osteoarthritis.
Doctors use medical history and physical exams to check for joint swelling and range of motion.
When non-drug treatments fail, joint replacement surgery can relieve pain and restore mobility.
Warm baths, hot packs, and maintaining a healthy weight can provide temporary relief from pain.
Imaging tests like X-rays can show bone spurs or a decrease in the space between bones in a joint.
Extra weight puts more stress on weight-bearing joints like knees and increases the risk of damage.
Cartilage is the slippery tissue that covers the ends of bones; in OA, this cartilage breaks down.
Strengthening the muscles around a joint helps support the joint and reduces pain.
Over-the-counter creams containing capsaicin or menthol can help soothe minor joint pain.
Advanced OA can lead to a total loss of joint function, making daily tasks like walking difficult.
As cartilage wears away, the body may grow extra bone (spurs) around the affected joint.
Previous injuries, such as from sports or accidents, can lead to osteoarthritis later in life.
Using canes, walkers, or shoe inserts can take pressure off joints and make movement easier.
Some people feel or hear a grating sensation (crepitus) when using the affected joint.
Some patients find relief through acupuncture or massage to manage chronic joint stiffness.
It is a degenerative joint disease where the joint structure gradually changes over time.
A UTI is an infection in any part of the urinary system, but most often occurs in the bladder.
Most UTIs are caused by bacteria entering the urethra and traveling into the bladder.
Symptoms include a strong, persistent urge to urinate and a burning sensation during urination.
Because most UTIs are bacterial, they are treated with bacteria-fighting medications called antibiotics.
Daily habits like wiping from front to back and staying hydrated can help prevent infections.
Women are at higher risk for UTIs, and the risk for both genders increases with age.
Infections often cause urine to appear cloudy, bloody, or have a strong, foul smell.
If left untreated, a bladder infection can spread to the kidneys, which is a much more serious condition.
Doctors diagnose a UTI by testing a urine sample for the presence of bacteria and white blood cells.
Drinking plenty of water helps flush bacteria out of the urinary tract before infection starts.
In women, UTIs often cause pain in the center of the pelvis and around the area of the pubic bone.
People who use catheters to urinate are at a much higher risk for developing recurring UTIs.
Kidney stones or an enlarged prostate can trap urine in the bladder, leading to infections.
Heating pads and drinking lots of fluids can help relieve discomfort while antibiotics work.
Cystitis is the medical term for an infection of the bladder, the most common type of UTI.
Changes in the vaginal flora and estrogen levels after menopause can increase UTI frequency.
Urinating shortly after sexual activity can help flush out bacteria that may have entered the urethra.
In older adults, a UTI may not cause typical symptoms but can lead to sudden confusion or behavior changes.
A urine culture identifies the specific type of bacteria causing the infection to choose the right antibiotic.
While most UTIs affect the bladder, they can also occur in the ureters or the kidneys.
